blocks.text: There is more reason in those who hold that חפרפרות chapharpheroth are moles in this passage, Es. II, 20. In that day a man shall cast away his idols of silver and his idols of gold, which he had made for himself to worship, לחפרפרות ולעטלפים, to the chaphorpheroth (or moles) and the bats. But much must be noted about this word. Let the first point [II, 449] be this: although it is a single word, it is nevertheless written separately, לחפר פרות, as if there were two words, as happens with some others. Thus at 2 Par. XXXIV, 6. in most [col. 1032] editions בחר בתיהם is written for בחרבותיהם, with their hammers. Ierem. XLVI, 20. יפה פיה for יפהפיה, most beautiful. Thren. IV, 3. כי ענים for כיענים, like ostriches; Ezech. XXVII, 6. בת אשורים for בתאשורים, of boxwood. The same happened with this word, so that it was split in two. Hence some explain it as though the words were separate: for instance, to the digger of fruits, as if it were a kind of bird so called because it pierces and bores through the fruits of trees; or to the digging of pits, as if פירות stood for חפירות, which is what the Hebrews call pits. But it is certain that the ancient interpreters, namely the Septuagint, the Elders, Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, Jerome, the Chaldee, the Syriac and the Arabic, read לחפרפרות as one word, since they rendered it by one word. Iarchius and Aben Ezra also hold that it is a single word. But this single word is explained in various ways. The Elders render τὰ μάταια [ta mataia], vain things; Aquila ὄρυγας [orygas], diggings; Symmachus ἄκαρπα [akarpa], fruitless things; Theodotion put the Hebrew word itself, ἀφαρφερώθ [apharpherōth]; the Chaldee טעותא, idols; the Syriac ܣܪܝܩܘܬܐ, vanities; Aben Ezra thinks it is שם עוף יעוף בלילה כעטלף ומביא עצמו ביום במקום סתר, the name of a bird which flies by night like a bat and by day withdraws into a hidden place. To weigh each of these is not for our present leisure ^{(6)}. It will suffice to point out that, deservedly, all of these are surpassed by Jerome among our writers, and among the Hebrews by R. Selomo, who understand moles here. For from the verb חפר chaphar, which means to dig, animals that are supremely ὀρυκτικὰ [oryktika], and that spend their whole life digging, are most fittingly named. And, as we already touched on in passing above ^{g)}, in חפרפרות chaphorpheroth the radicals are doubled so that the meaning may be intensified. So too אדמדם adamdem for intensely red; ירקרק jerakrak for intensely yellow; שחרחר secharchor for very dark; עקלקל akalkal for exceedingly winding; הפכפך haphachphach for exceedingly changeable; פתלתל pethalthol for exceedingly twisted; יפהפיה jephephija for exceedingly beautiful. Moreover, this same rendering joins moles with bats, which are animals alike in many respects, although the one creeps beneath the earth and the other rises into the air in flight. First, both are lowly and unclean little animals. Second, both are in some way referred to the mouse kind. This has already been proved of the mole ^{h)}, and in the case of the bat it is known to everyone. Hence in Nonius, Varro says in the Agathon: I have become a bat; I am neither wholly among the mice nor among the birds. In Aesop a bat, caught by a weasel as a bird, [II, 450] in order to escape ἔλεγεν, ὀυκ ὄρνις, ἀλλὰ μῦς εἶναι [elegen, ouk ornis, alla mys einai], said that it was not a bird but a mouse. Scaliger maintains that it has a nature midway between the shrew and the swallow. Accordingly in Eustathius τρισμὸς [trismos] is common to the mouse and the bat. And Victorinus in his book De orthographia calls the bat sorex avis [bird-shrew]; Kimchi calls it העטלף בעל כנפים, a winged mouse; the Lombards ratto penago, that is, feathered mouse; the Spaniards morcego, that is, blind mouse; the French chauve-souris, that is, bald shrew. Third, the mole is blind, and the bat sees little. Hence in Arabic it is خغاش [khughāsh] chuphas. For خغش [khaghash] chaphas among them denotes smallness and weakness of the eyes, and اخغش [akhghash] achphaso is μύωψ [myōps]. Accordingly, as moles live beneath the earth, so bats spend the day in caves and dark places.
— — — and, hating the light, they fly by night, and take their name from the late evening ^{i)}.
